source_note: Allen Hatcher, Algebraic Topology, Cambridge University Press, 2002 (electronic version as distributed from the author's Cornell page; the local file includes the 2015 reprinting corrections note). Local file Hatcher-2002-AlgebraicTopology.pdf, 8,121,741 bytes, full sha256 4b8826864039ee4aee077f7868aae0749854ded6f357505ddf22ef1bc07cf527, book_id is the first 16 hex chars of the scan digest sha256(str(size) + file bytes). Extracted text is clean and complete (about 1.77 million characters, 27,787 lines) with only routine line break hyphenation and occasional superscript layout artifacts in displayed formulas; all 35 verbatim quotes were machine checked as contiguous substrings of the extracted text under whitespace, dehyphenation, ligature, and quote normalization. No catalog corrections needed. Motif-lane extraction (MOTIF-TIERB-DRAIN-01) of the same work for sync-cloud reconciliation.

primitives.name: A homotopy is a continuous one-parameter family of maps ft : X to Y, packaged as a single continuous map on X cross I
primitives.verbatim_quote: which is simply any family of maps ft : X →Y , t ∈ I , such that the associated map F : X × I →Y given by F (x, t) = ft (x) is continuous.
primitives.page: Chapter 0, Homotopy and Homotopy Type (text line 338)
assumptions: Maps are continuous by the book's standing convention
The parameter t ranges over the unit interval I = [0, 1]
primitives.breakdown_regime: Continuity of the assembled map F : X x I to Y is the whole content; a pointwise family of continuous maps that is not jointly continuous is not a homotopy

layer2.mapping: Two model states count as the same when one deforms continuously into the other; the engine can treat scenario families connected by a continuous deformation as one equivalence class rather than independent cases
layer2.telemetry: Continuous scenario deformations in the simulation layer: parameter sweeps over weather, rest, and venue inputs

primitives.name: A deformation retraction shrinks a space onto a subspace through maps fixing the subspace, starting at the identity and ending at a retraction
primitives.verbatim_quote: A deformation retraction of a space X onto a subspace A is a family of maps ft : X →X , t ∈ I , such that f0 = 11 (the identity map), f1 (X) = A , and ft || A = 11 for all t . The family ft should be continuous in the sense that the associated map X × I →X , (x, t) ֏ ft (x) , is continuous.
primitives.page: Chapter 0, Homotopy and Homotopy Type (text line 298)
assumptions: The subspace A is held pointwise fixed for all t
f0 is the identity and f1 maps X onto A
primitives.breakdown_regime: Not every retraction arises this way; a space retracting onto a point need not deformation retract onto it, and spaces with holes obstruct point retractions entirely

layer2.mapping: A full feature space that deformation retracts onto a smaller core is a license to reason on the core alone; the engine can compress a state space onto a skeleton when a structure preserving shrink exists
layer2.telemetry: Feature-space reduction audits: which signal families collapse onto a retained core without changing conclusions

primitives.name: Maps f and g inverse up to homotopy make X and Y homotopy equivalent, the book's basic notion of same shape
primitives.verbatim_quote: a map f : X →Y is called a homotopy equivalence if there is a map g : Y →X such that f g ≃ 11 and gf ≃ 11. The spaces X and Y are said to be homotopy equivalent or to have the same homotopy type.
primitives.page: Chapter 0, Homotopy and Homotopy Type (text line 313)
assumptions: Both compositions fg and gf need only be homotopic to identity maps, not equal to them
primitives.breakdown_regime: Strictly weaker than homeomorphism and strictly stronger than having isomorphic invariants in general; two spaces can share all homology groups without being homotopy equivalent

layer2.mapping: Equivalence up to tolerated deformation is the right sameness notion for reasoning states: two game scripts that differ only by noise-level reorderings should hash to the same engine state
layer2.telemetry: State canonicalization keys in the reasoning trace store: deformation tolerant hashing of game states

primitives.name: A CW complex is a space built inductively by attaching cells of increasing dimension along maps from spheres, with the weak topology
primitives.verbatim_quote: A space X constructed in this way is called a cell complex or CW complex.
assumptions: Attaching maps are continuous; the topology is the weak topology with respect to the skeleta
primitives.breakdown_regime: The class is broad but not universal: arbitrary wild spaces need CW approximation before the book's computational machinery applies cleanly

layer2.mapping: Layered construction from atomic cells is the engine's own build pattern: base objects first, then attachments of higher order structure along specified gluing maps, each layer inheriting only what the attaching maps carry
layer2.telemetry: Engine build graph: which composite signals attach to which base signals, and along which interfaces

primitives.name: For a finite cell complex the Euler characteristic is the alternating count of cells: even-dimensional cells minus odd-dimensional cells
primitives.verbatim_quote: the Euler characteristic, which for a cell complex with finitely many cells is defined to be the number of even-dimensional cells minus the number of odd-dimensional cells.
assumptions: The complex has finitely many cells
The count uses cells of the chosen structure, though the value is later proved structure independent
primitives.breakdown_regime: Defined here only for finite complexes; for infinite complexes the alternating sum may diverge and needs the homological definition instead

layer2.mapping: An alternating sum over a layered decomposition is a cheap global invariant; the engine can keep parity style checksums over layered signal counts that must stay fixed when the decomposition changes
layer2.telemetry: Bookkeeping checksums over the weekly layer stack: usage, health, matchup, situation counts by layer parity

primitives.name: Real projective n space has one cell in each dimension 0 through n, each attached by the quotient projection from the sphere
primitives.verbatim_quote: It follows by induction on n that RPn has a cell complex structure e0 ∪ e1 ∪ ··· ∪ en with one cell ei in each dimension i ≤ n .
assumptions: RPn is the quotient of the sphere by antipodal identification
Induction on n supplies the attaching maps
primitives.breakdown_regime: Specific to projective spaces; general spaces can need many cells per dimension and the minimal cell count is itself a hard invariant

layer2.mapping: A quotient by a symmetry can admit a dramatically smaller cell decomposition than the original object; the engine should look for symmetry quotients of its state space before paying for the full representation
layer2.telemetry: Symmetry detection in matchup state spaces: mirrored formations and left right flipped alignments

primitives.name: A path is a continuous map from the unit interval into the space, the primitive trajectory from which loops and homotopies are built
primitives.verbatim_quote: By a path in a space X we mean a continuous map f : I →X where I is the unit interval [0, 1] .
assumptions: I is the unit interval [0, 1]
Continuity is with respect to the topology of X
primitives.breakdown_regime: A path records no speed or parametrization invariant information; reparametrized paths are different maps carrying the same geometric trace

layer2.mapping: The engine's basic unit is likewise a parametrized trajectory through a state space: a drive, a possession sequence, a game script; everything else is built by composing and deforming these
layer2.telemetry: Play by play and drive level trajectory records with fixed endpoints: score state and field position at start and end

primitives.name: Paths with fixed endpoints are homotopic when a homotopy of paths joins them, and the linear homotopy joins any two paths in Euclidean space
primitives.verbatim_quote: When two paths f0 and f1 are connected in this way by a homotopy ft , they are said to be homotopic. The notation for this is f0 ≃ f1 .
assumptions: Endpoints are held fixed throughout the homotopy
The straight line formula requires a convex ambient space so the segments stay inside X
primitives.breakdown_regime: Fails outside convex sets: in a space with a hole, two paths around opposite sides of the hole are not homotopic, which is exactly the phenomenon the fundamental group detects

layer2.mapping: Interpolating between two trajectories is only valid when the ambient space has no obstruction between them; the engine must check for holes, meaning forbidden or unreachable intermediate states, before averaging two game scripts
layer2.telemetry: Trajectory interpolation validity flags in scenario blending: whether intermediate states are reachable

symbol_and_unit_ledger.f_0, f_1: the two paths being joined, maps I to R^n (dimensionless)

primitives.name: Homotopy classes of loops at a basepoint form a group under path composition: this is the fundamental group pi1(X, x0)
primitives.verbatim_quote: Proposition 1.3. π1 (X, x0 ) is a group with respect to the product [f ][g] = [f g] . This group is called the fundamental group of X at the basepoint x0 .
assumptions: Loops share the fixed basepoint x0 so the product is always defined
Homotopy classes, not individual loops, are the group elements
primitives.breakdown_regime: Depends on the basepoint up to isomorphism only when X is path connected; for disconnected or badly based spaces the group is a groupoid level object instead

layer2.mapping: Sequences of events compose, and two sequences are the same engine object when one deforms into the other without changing endpoints; the algebra of drives and possessions is a group like structure over script classes
layer2.telemetry: Drive sequence composition logs: concatenated possession scripts with start and end game states

symbol_and_unit_ledger.[f], [g]: homotopy classes of loops based at x0 (dimensionless)
symbol_and_unit_ledger.fg: the composite loop traversing f then g at double speed (dimensionless)

primitives.name: The fundamental group of the circle is infinite cyclic, generated by the once around loop: every loop is homotopic to a unique winding power
primitives.verbatim_quote: Theorem 1.7. π1 (S 1 ) is an infinite cyclic group generated by the homotopy class of the loop ω(s) = (cos 2π s, sin 2π s) based at (1, 0) .
assumptions: The generator is the loop omega(s) = (cos 2 pi s, sin 2 pi s) based at (1, 0)
Uniqueness of the winding number n in Z is the content of the theorem
primitives.breakdown_regime: The first nontrivial fundamental group computation; the method, lifting to the real line cover, does not directly compute pi1 for general spaces

layer2.mapping: A cyclic process is classified by a single integer winding count; the engine can classify periodic game rhythms, rotation cycles, and snap count cycles by one integer invariant instead of a full history
layer2.telemetry: Cycle counters: rotation patterns, play call cycles, and tempo periods per team per game

symbol_and_unit_ledger.\\mathbb{Z}: the infinite cyclic group of winding numbers (dimensionless)

primitives.name: Every continuous map from the 2 disk to itself has a fixed point, proved by showing a retraction onto the circle would kill pi1 of the circle
primitives.verbatim_quote: Theorem 1.9. Every continuous map h : D2 →D2 has a fixed point, that is, a point x ∈ D 2 with h(x) = x .
assumptions: The map h : D2 to D2 is continuous
The proof is by contradiction through the nonexistence of a retraction D2 to S1
primitives.breakdown_regime: Stated and proved here in dimension 2 via pi1; higher dimensions need degree or homology, and the statement fails for maps of open disks or discontinuous maps

layer2.mapping: Self referential update rules on a closed state region must have a fixed point; an engine adjustment loop that maps a bounded rating region into itself cannot push every state, so equilibrium ratings exist and iteration can be aimed at them
layer2.telemetry: Iterative rating update logs: whether successive rating vectors are converging toward a fixed vector

primitives.name: Van Kampen: pi1 of a union of open path connected sets is the free product of the pieces' groups modulo the identifications forced by their intersections
primitives.verbatim_quote: Theorem 1.20. If X is the union of path-connected open sets Aα each containing the basepoint x0 ∈ X and if each intersection Aα ∩ Aβ is path-connected, then the homomorphism Φ : ∗α π1 (Aα )→π1 (X) is surjective. If in addition each intersection Aα ∩ Aβ ∩ Aγ is path-connected, then the kernel of Φ is the normal subgroup N generated by all elements of the form iαβ (ω)iβα (ω)−1 for ω ∈ π1 (Aα ∩ Aβ ) , and hence Φ induces an isomorphism π1 (X) ≈ ∗α π1 (Aα )/N .
assumptions: Each A_alpha is open and path connected and contains the basepoint
Pairwise intersections are path connected for surjectivity, triple intersections for the kernel description
primitives.breakdown_regime: Hypotheses fail for closed decompositions or disconnected overlaps, where pi1 of the union is not determined by the pieces in this form

layer2.mapping: Local analyses combine into a global one by taking all local conclusions freely, then quotienting by exactly the relations the overlaps force; this is the engine's rule for merging regional matchup reads into one global read without double counting the shared region
layer2.telemetry: Overlap registry for layered reads: which signals are shared between the usage, health, and matchup layers

symbol_and_unit_ledger.*_\\alpha \\pi_1(A_\\alpha): free product of the fundamental groups of the covering pieces (dimensionless)
symbol_and_unit_ledger.N: normal subgroup generated by i_{\alpha\beta}(\omega) i_{\beta\alpha}(\omega)^{-1} for loops in the overlaps (dimensionless)

primitives.name: A covering space maps onto X so that every point has a neighborhood whose preimage is a disjoint union of sheets, each mapped homeomorphically down
primitives.verbatim_quote: A covering space of a space X is a space X with a map p : Xe →X satisfying the following condition: Each point x ∈ X has an open neighborhood U in X such that p −1 (U) is a union of disjoint open sets in X e, each of which is mapped homeomorphically onto U by p .
assumptions: The evenly covered neighborhood condition holds at every point of X
The number of sheets is locally constant, hence constant on connected X
primitives.breakdown_regime: The local homeomorphism condition is strong: branched covers and maps with fold points are excluded, and p need not be surjective under the book's convention

layer2.mapping: A many sheeted representation over one base state, with each sheet locally identical to the base, is the engine's picture of scenario branching: many full scenarios lying over one observed game state, distinguished only globally
layer2.telemetry: Scenario branch registry: full alternative game continuations indexed over one observed state

primitives.name: Covering spaces lift homotopies uniquely: a homotopy downstairs plus a lift of its start determines a unique lifted homotopy
primitives.verbatim_quote: Proposition 1.30. Given a covering space p : Xe →X , a homotopy ft : Y →X , and a map fe0 : Y →X e lifting f0 , then there exists a unique homotopy fet : Y →X e of fe0 that lifts ft .
assumptions: p is a covering space
The initial lift fe0 of f0 is given
primitives.breakdown_regime: Uniqueness is the force of the statement; for general maps lifts may fail to exist or branch, and the property characterizes coverings among local homeomorphisms under mild hypotheses

layer2.mapping: Given a base trajectory and one starting branch, the whole lifted trajectory is forced; the engine can propagate a chosen scenario branch along an observed game timeline without re-deciding the branch at each step
layer2.telemetry: Branch consistent scenario propagation: one selected continuation carried along the observed play sequence

primitives.name: Connected covering spaces of X correspond to subgroups of pi1(X), the Galois correspondence of covering space theory
primitives.verbatim_quote: The main thrust of the classification will be a correspondence between connected covering spaces of X and subgroups of π1 (X) . This is often called the Galois correspondence because of its surprising similarity to another basic correspondence in the purely algebraic subject of Galois theory.
primitives.page: Section 1.3, The Classification of Covering Spaces (text line 3170)
assumptions: X is connected and locally path connected
Based covers correspond to actual subgroups, unbased covers to conjugacy classes
primitives.breakdown_regime: Requires the base to admit the covers in question; existence of a universal cover needs semilocal simple connectedness, which wild spaces can fail

layer2.mapping: The set of consistent global scenarios over a state is classified by an algebraic object attached to the state; the engine can index its scenario lattice by subgroup like keys instead of enumerating scenarios
layer2.telemetry: Scenario lattice index: algebraic keys classifying families of continuations over a game state

primitives.name: Simplicial homology assigns to a Delta complex the homology of the chain complex built from its simplices, the book's computable first model of homology
primitives.verbatim_quote: Our goal now is to define the simplicial homology groups of a ∆ complex X .
assumptions: The space carries a Delta complex structure with ordered vertices on each simplex
primitives.breakdown_regime: Depends a priori on the chosen Delta structure; agreement with singular homology is a theorem, not a definition, and spaces without such structures are outside its direct reach

layer2.mapping: Start with the finite combinatorial model where computation is possible, then prove the invariant does not depend on the model; the engine should prototype every new signal on a finite discretized version before trusting it on raw data
layer2.telemetry: Discretized prototypes: binned versions of continuous signals used for first pass validation

primitives.name: The boundary of a simplex is the alternating sum of its faces: d[v0,v1,v2] = [v1,v2] - [v0,v2] + [v0,v1]
assumptions: Vertices carry a fixed ordering that determines the signs
Faces are the characteristic maps restricted to the codimension one faces
primitives.breakdown_regime: The sign convention is essential: without alternating signs the boundary of a boundary does not cancel and no homology results

layer2.mapping: A composite object decomposes into signed boundary pieces whose contributions cancel in pairs one level down; the engine's drive decomposition into plays has the same telescoping structure, where internal boundaries cancel and only endpoints survive
layer2.telemetry: Telescoping checks in drive accounting: intermediate states cancel, net change equals endpoints

symbol_and_unit_ledger.[v_0, v_1, v_2]: the oriented 2 simplex on vertices v0, v1, v2 (dimensionless)
symbol_and_unit_ledger.[v_i, v_j]: the oriented edge face opposite the deleted vertex (dimensionless)
symbol_and_unit_ledger.(-1)^i signs: orientation signs making faces coherently oriented (dimensionless)

primitives.name: A chain complex is a sequence of groups and boundary maps with d squared zero; its homology is cycles modulo boundaries
primitives.verbatim_quote: Such a sequence is called a chain complex. Note that we have extended the sequence by a 0 at the right end, with ∂0 = 0 . The equation ∂n ∂n+1 = 0 is equivalent to the inclusion Im ∂n+1 ⊂ Ker ∂n , where Im and Ker denote image and kernel. So we can define the n th homology group of the chain complex to be the quotient group Hn = Ker ∂n / Im ∂n+1 .
assumptions: The relation d_n d_{n+1} = 0 holds for every n
Groups are abelian in this treatment
primitives.breakdown_regime: Homology sees only the quotient: two cycles differing by a boundary are identified, so information inside a boundary class is deliberately discarded

layer2.mapping: The engine's core quotient: patterns that are boundaries, meaning fully explained by one level up, are divided out, and what remains is the unexplained residue worth reasoning about; homology is the formal version of residual analysis
layer2.telemetry: Residual registries: observed patterns minus the patterns explained by the layer above, per signal family

symbol_and_unit_ledger.\\partial_n: boundary homomorphism from n chains to (n-1) chains (dimensionless)
symbol_and_unit_ledger.\\ker \\partial_n: the cycles: chains with zero boundary (dimensionless)
symbol_and_unit_ledger.\\operatorname{im} \\partial_{n+1}: the boundaries: chains that bound one dimension up (dimensionless)

primitives.name: A singular n simplex is just a continuous map from the standard simplex into X, allowed to be arbitrarily degenerate or self overlapping
primitives.verbatim_quote: A singular n simplex in a space X is by definition just a map σ : ∆n →X . The word ‘singular’ is used here to express the idea that σ need not be a nice embedding but can have ‘singularities’ where its image does not look at all like a simplex. All that is required is that σ be continuous.
assumptions: Continuity is the only requirement on the map
The standard simplex carries its canonical vertex ordering
primitives.breakdown_regime: The chain groups are enormous, usually uncountable rank, so singular homology is a theoretical device whose computations always route through finite models

layer2.mapping: Probe a space with maps from a standard test object rather than with intrinsic pieces; the engine likewise probes a matchup with standard test scenarios mapped in, instead of waiting for naturally occurring examples
layer2.telemetry: Standard probe scenarios: a fixed battery of test situations applied to every matchup

primitives.name: Because d squared is zero for singular chains, singular homology Hn(X) = ker d / im d is defined for every space with no chosen structure
primitives.verbatim_quote: The proof of Lemma 2.1 applies equally well to singular simplices, showing that ∂n ∂n+1 = 0 or more concisely ∂ 2 = 0 , so we can define the singular homology group Hn (X) = Ker ∂n / Im ∂n+1 .
assumptions: Lemma 2.1's cancellation argument applies verbatim to singular simplices
primitives.breakdown_regime: Well defined for all spaces but computable only through comparison theorems: excision, Mayer Vietoris, and cellular homology do the actual work

layer2.mapping: Define the invariant on the largest possible domain first, even when it is not directly computable, then earn computation through comparison results; the engine should define signals on all games first and approximate second
layer2.telemetry: Signal coverage ledger: signals defined league wide versus signals only computable on a subset

symbol_and_unit_ledger.\\partial_n: boundary map on singular n chains (dimensionless)
symbol_and_unit_ledger.H_n(X): n th singular homology group of X (dimensionless)

primitives.name: Homeomorphic spaces have isomorphic singular homology groups, directly from the definition, unlike simplicial homology
primitives.verbatim_quote: It is evident from the definition that homeomorphic spaces have isomorphic singular homology groups Hn , in contrast with the situation for Hn∆ .
assumptions: A homeomorphism induces maps on singular simplices in both directions
primitives.breakdown_regime: Invariance under the much weaker relation of homotopy equivalence is true but requires proof through chain homotopies; it does not follow from the definition alone

layer2.mapping: An invariant worth trusting must be unchanged under relabelings of the underlying object; the engine should test every new metric under renaming and reordering of its inputs before adoption
layer2.telemetry: Invariance test suite: metric values under permuted and relabeled inputs

primitives.name: The relative homology groups of a pair (X, A) fit into a long exact sequence linking the homology of A, of X, and of the pair
primitives.verbatim_quote: Our goal now is to show that the relative homology groups Hn (X, A) for any pair (X, A) fit into a long exact sequence
primitives.page: Section 2.1, Homotopy Properties of Chain Complexes (text line 5888)
assumptions: Relative groups are homology of the quotient chain complex C(X)/C(A)
primitives.breakdown_regime: Exactness is the content: the sequence constrains but does not by itself determine the groups, and extension problems remain when reading off a middle group

layer2.mapping: Part, whole, and relative difference form one exact chain of accounts: knowing two constrains the third; the engine's layer accounting should be exact in this sense, with discrepancies forced to appear somewhere named
layer2.telemetry: Layer reconciliation: team level, unit level, and matchup relative numbers tied in one sequence

primitives.name: Excision: deleting a subset Z whose closure lies inside the interior of A does not change the relative homology of the pair (X, A)
primitives.verbatim_quote:
A fundamental property of relative homology groups is given by the following
Excision Theorem, describing when the relative groups Hn (X, A) are unaffected by
deleting, or excising, a subset Z ⊂ A .
primitives.page: Section 2.2, prose lead-in to Theorem 2.20 (text line 6086)
assumptions: The closure of Z is contained in the interior of A
Equivalently, the interiors of A and B cover X in the second formulation
primitives.breakdown_regime: The closure inside interior hypothesis is sharp: excising a set that touches the boundary of A can change relative homology

layer2.mapping: Data buried strictly inside a region already accounted for can be removed without changing the relative conclusion; the engine may drop plays strictly interior to a decided region of the analysis when computing relative effects
layer2.telemetry: Excision log: plays removed from relative computations with the interior containment check recorded

primitives.name: The Mayer Vietoris sequence computes homology of a union from the homology of two pieces and their intersection, the homology analog of van Kampen
primitives.verbatim_quote: In addition to the long exact sequence of homology groups for a pair (X, A) , there is another sort of long exact sequence, known as a Mayer–Vietoris sequence, which is equally powerful but is sometimes more convenient to use.
assumptions: X is the union of the interiors of A and B
The sequence is the long exact sequence of the associated short exact sequence of chain complexes
primitives.breakdown_regime: Needs the interior covering condition; for unions along badly overlapping closed sets the sequence can fail, and it determines H(X) only up to the extension data in the sequence

layer2.mapping: Two partial analyses plus their overlap determine the whole, with the overlap entering twice signed; the engine merges split analyses, first half and second half or home and road, by the same inclusion accounting
layer2.telemetry: Split merge worksheets: two partial samples plus their shared games, combined with overlap correction

primitives.name: The cellular chain complex has one generator per cell and boundary maps from the skeletal exact sequences, and its homology is the homology of X
primitives.verbatim_quote: Thus the horizontal row in the diagram is a chain complex, called the cellular chain complex of X since Hn (X n , X n−1 ) is free with basis in one-to-one correspondence with the n cells of X , so one can think of elements of Hn (X n , X n−1 ) as linear combinations of n cells of X .
assumptions: X is a CW complex with skeleta X^n
Hn(X^n, X^{n-1}) is free on the n cells
primitives.breakdown_regime: The boundary maps are degrees of attaching maps composed with projections, which can be hard to extract for geometrically complicated attaching maps

layer2.mapping: Replace a huge theoretical chain complex by one generator per structural atom and compute there; the engine's per play and per drive atoms play the cell role, and aggregate invariants should be computed on the atomic complex
layer2.telemetry: Atomic computation layer: per play generators feeding aggregate invariant calculations

primitives.name: The local degree of a map at a preimage point is plus or minus 1 when the map is locally a homeomorphism, and global degree is the sum of local degrees
primitives.verbatim_quote: For example, if f is a homeomorphism, then y can be any point and there is only one corresponding xi , so all the maps in the diagram are isomorphisms and deg f || xi = deg f = ±1 .
assumptions: The point y is chosen with finitely many preimages xi in the argument
Excision identifies the local groups with Hn(S^n) = Z
primitives.breakdown_regime: For maps that fold or branch at xi the local degree can be any integer and sign determination needs orientation care; the sum formula needs the preimage finite

layer2.mapping: A global multiplicity is the sum of signed local multiplicities; the engine can compute a global tendency as a sum of signed local contributions, each auditable on its own neighborhood
layer2.telemetry: Local contribution ledgers: per matchup or per drive signed contributions summing to the global number

primitives.name: The Euler characteristic equals the alternating sum of the ranks of the homology groups, hence depends only on homotopy type
primitives.verbatim_quote: The following result shows that χ (X) can be defined purely in terms of homology, and hence depends only on the homotopy type of X . In particular, χ (X) is independent of the choice of CW structure on X .
assumptions: X has finitely generated homology and a finite CW structure
Rank additivity over short exact sequences of finitely generated abelian groups
primitives.breakdown_regime: Torsion in homology is invisible to chi; two spaces with different torsion can share an Euler characteristic

layer2.mapping: The same alternating checksum can be computed from the decomposition or from the invariants, and the two must agree; the engine should compute its headline numbers by two independent routes and treat disagreement as a defect
layer2.telemetry: Dual route computation checks: headline metrics computed from raw atoms and from aggregated invariants

symbol_and_unit_ledger.rank H_n(X): number of Z summands in the n th homology group (dimensionless)

primitives.name: Cohomology with arbitrary coefficients is determined by integral homology through split exact sequences involving Hom and Ext terms
primitives.verbatim_quote: This is known as the universal coefficient theorem for cohomology because it is formally analogous to the universal coefficient theorem for homology in §3.A which expresses homology with arbitrary coefficients in terms of homology with Z coefficients.
assumptions: The chain complex consists of free abelian groups
The sequences split, though the splitting is not natural
primitives.breakdown_regime: The Ext term is the obstruction to cohomology being a simple dual of homology; torsion in homology one degree down creates cohomology that Hom alone misses

layer2.mapping: Changing the coefficient lens on the same underlying data creates predictable new terms from old torsion; the engine should expect new views of the same data to reveal exactly the previously hidden residual classes, no more and no less
layer2.telemetry: View change audits: what new structure appears when the same data is rescored under a different lens

primitives.name: The cup product multiplies cohomology classes by evaluating the factors on the front and back faces of a simplex, making cohomology a ring
primitives.verbatim_quote: To define the cup product we consider cohomology with coefficients in a ring R , the most common choices being Z , Zn , and Q .
assumptions: Coefficients lie in a ring R so the product of values is defined
The Leibniz rule for the coboundary makes the product descend to cohomology classes
primitives.breakdown_regime: The product can vanish for degree reasons or torsion reasons even on spaces with rich homology; it detects linking phenomena that additive invariants miss

layer2.mapping: Two signals can be multiplied, not just added, by evaluating each on its own segment of the same underlying event; the engine's interaction terms should be built as products over complementary segments of one play or drive
layer2.telemetry: Interaction term construction: front segment and back segment factor values over the same drive

symbol_and_unit_ledger.\\varphi, \\psi: cochains of degrees k and l with values in the ring R (dimensionless)
symbol_and_unit_ledger.[v_0, \\dots, v_k]: front k face of the simplex (dimensionless)
symbol_and_unit_ledger.[v_k, \\dots, v_{k+\\ell}]: back l face sharing the vertex v_k (dimensionless)

primitives.name: Poincare duality: on a closed orientable n manifold, cap product with the fundamental class is an isomorphism from H^k to H_{n-k}
primitives.verbatim_quote:
The form of Poincaré duality we will prove asserts that for an R orientable closed
n manifold, a certain naturally defined map H k (M; R)→Hn−k (M; R) is an isomor-
phism. The definition of this map will be in terms of a more general construction
called cap product, which has close connections with cup product.
primitives.page: Section 3.3, 'The Duality Theorem' lead-in (text line 12075); formal statement Theorem 3.30
assumptions: M is closed, meaning compact without boundary
M is R orientable and carries a fundamental class
primitives.breakdown_regime: Fails for noncompact or nonorientable manifolds in this form; boundary manifolds need the relative Lefschetz form instead

layer2.mapping: On a closed system, the high order view and the low order view determine each other through one pairing with the whole; the engine can cross check its micro reads against its macro reads by a duality style pairing with the full game
layer2.telemetry: Micro macro cross checks: player level and team level reads paired against the complete game record

symbol_and_unit_ledger.D: the duality isomorphism H^k(M; R) to H_{n-k}(M; R) (dimensionless)

primitives.name: For n at least 2 the homotopy groups pi_n are always abelian, and relative homotopy groups fit into long exact sequences like homology
primitives.verbatim_quote: For example, πn (X) turns out to be always abelian for n ≥ 2 , and there are relative homotopy groups fitting into a long exact sequence just like the long exact sequence of homology groups.
assumptions: n is at least 2 for commutativity
Basepoints are fixed throughout
primitives.breakdown_regime: Higher homotopy groups lack both excision and a van Kampen theorem, which is why they are far harder to compute than pi1 or homology

layer2.mapping: Once a classification has two independent directions of variation, order stops mattering; the engine should detect when its sequential reads commute, because commuting reads can be parallelized and reordered safely
layer2.telemetry: Commutativity probes: whether swapping the order of two analysis passes changes the output

primitives.name: Whitehead's theorem: a map between connected CW complexes inducing isomorphisms on all homotopy groups is a homotopy equivalence
primitives.verbatim_quote:
One reason for this is Whitehead’s theorem that a map between
CW complexes which induces isomorphisms on all homotopy groups is a homotopy
equivalence.
primitives.page: Chapter 4 introduction, prose statement (text line 17128); formal statement Theorem 4.5, Section 4.1
assumptions: X and Y are connected CW complexes
Isomorphisms are required on pi_n for every n, at every basepoint in the unconnected case
primitives.breakdown_regime: False for general spaces: weak homotopy equivalences between non CW spaces need not be homotopy equivalences, and isomorphic homotopy groups without a map do not suffice

layer2.mapping: If a proposed identification of two states respects every level of the invariant tower, the identification is real; the engine can promote a candidate state matching to an equality only after it survives checks at every resolution level
layer2.telemetry: Promotion gate for state identifications: agreement at play, drive, game, and season resolution

primitives.name: The Hurewicz theorem: for an (n-1) connected space the first nonzero homotopy and homology groups occur together and pi_n is isomorphic to H_n
primitives.verbatim_quote: Theorem 4.32. If a space X is (n − 1) connected, n ≥ 2 , then He i (X) = 0 for i < n and πn (X) ≈ Hn (X) .
assumptions: X is (n - 1) connected with n at least 2
The relative case also needs A simply connected and nonempty
primitives.breakdown_regime: Beyond the first nonzero dimension there is no nice relation: spheres have trivial homology above n but rich higher homotopy, and Eilenberg MacLane spaces show the reverse

layer2.mapping: The first level at which a system shows any signal is the level where the intuitive and the computable invariants coincide; the engine should locate the first nonzero layer of a new signal family, because there the cheap computation is exact
layer2.telemetry: First signal layer detection: the coarsest resolution at which a new family registers anything

primitives.name: A fibration is a map with the homotopy lifting property for all spaces, generalizing covering spaces and product projections
primitives.verbatim_quote: A fibration is a map p : E →B having the homotopy lifting property with respect to all spaces X .
assumptions: Lifts exist for homotopies from every test space X
A projection B x F to B is the trivial example
primitives.breakdown_regime: The full strength is often more than is available; Serre fibrations, with lifting only for disks, are the working notion and still yield the long exact sequence

layer2.mapping: A projection from a total state to a summary is well behaved when every deformation of the summary lifts to the total state; the engine should only trust summary statistics whose changes can be realized by actual full states
layer2.telemetry: Liftability checks for summaries: whether a changed aggregate corresponds to a realizable full record

primitives.name: A weak homotopy equivalence induces isomorphisms on all homotopy groups, and between CW complexes Whitehead's theorem upgrades it to a homotopy equivalence
primitives.verbatim_quote: Whitehead’s theorem can be restated as saying that a weak homotopy equivalence between CW complexes is a homotopy equivalence.
assumptions: Isomorphisms on pi_n are required for all n and all basepoints
primitives.breakdown_regime: Between arbitrary spaces the upgrade fails: there are weak homotopy equivalences, like a map from a wild space to a point, that are not homotopy equivalences

layer2.mapping: Agreement on every tested invariant is the weak form of sameness and is exactly what an engine can ever check; the CW hypothesis is the reminder that the upgrade to true sameness needs the objects to be built from tame pieces
layer2.telemetry: Tameness registry: which engine objects are built from standard pieces and so qualify for invariant based identification

reasoning_traces.think: This book is the classical architecture of algebraic topology presented as one connected machine, and reading it whole shows how deliberately each part loads the next. Chapter 0 sets the working equivalence relation. Homotopy, deformation retraction, and homotopy equivalence replace the rigid notion of homeomorphism with sameness up to continuous deformation, and CW complexes supply the class of spaces on which everything later can actually be computed. The fundamental group of Chapter 1 is the first invariant built on this foundation: loops at a basepoint, composed by concatenation and divided by homotopy, give a group that already distinguishes linked from unlinked circles and proves the Brouwer fixed point theorem in dimension two. Its two computational engines are van Kampen's theorem, which assembles the group of a union from the groups of pieces and the relations forced by overlaps, and covering space theory, where the homotopy lifting property turns geometry into algebra and culminates in the Galois correspondence between connected covers and subgroups. Chapter 2 rebuilds the same philosophy one level more algebraically. Simplicial homology on Delta complexes makes the boundary operator concrete: an alternating sum of faces with the miraculous cancellation that the boundary of a boundary is zero. Singular homology then frees the definition from any chosen decomposition, and the chain complex language, cycles modulo boundaries, becomes the permanent grammar. Around this core the chapter arranges the tools that make homology computable in practice: the long exact sequence of a pair, excision, Mayer Vietoris, cellular homology with one generator per cell, degree as a sum of local degrees, and the Euler characteristic recovered from homology ranks. Chapter 3 dualizes. Cohomology is homology read through Hom, corrected by Ext in the universal coefficient theorem, and then enriched beyond homology by the cup product, which makes cohomology a ring and detects linking that additive invariants cannot see. Cap product with a fundamental class gives Poincare duality, the statement that on a closed orientable manifold the high and low dimensional views determine each other completely. Chapter 4 returns to homotopy with the higher groups, where the tone changes: the groups are abelian and fit into exact sequences, Whitehead's theorem says they completely determine maps between CW complexes, and the Hurewicz theorem ties the first nonzero homotopy group to the first nonzero homology group, but excision and van Kampen fail and computation becomes genuinely hard. Fibrations restore some order by giving long exact sequences for bundles. For a reasoning engine the transferable content is the discipline of the whole design. Define an invariant on the largest honest domain, prove it does not depend on auxiliary choices, build finite combinatorial models where computation is possible, merge local computations through overlap corrections, quotient out whatever is explained one level up, and know exactly which theorems fail at the frontier so the failure is a boundary marker rather than a surprise. The book also teaches a standard of proof hygiene: every major invariant here is accompanied by the precise hypotheses under which its computation rules work, and the counterexamples at the edges, wild spaces, non CW complexes, disconnected overlaps, are treated as part of the theory rather than as embarrassments. The middle chapters reward a second, slower reading because their theorems form a dependency graph that is itself instructive. Excision is proved by barycentric subdivision, the technique of cutting chains into arbitrarily small pieces until they fit inside a chosen cover, and this same subdivision idea quietly powers the equivalence between the small chain complex used for Mayer Vietoris and the full singular complex. Cellular homology is then derived, not defined into existence: the long exact sequences of consecutive skeleta are stacked into a diagram, the cellular boundary emerges as a composition of a boundary map and a projection, and the theorem that cellular homology equals singular homology converts every CW computation into finite linear algebra over the integers. Degree illustrates the local to global pattern in its purest form, since the global degree of a map between spheres is defined through homology but computed by summing signed local contributions at the preimages of a single well chosen point. The cohomology chapter changes what an invariant can be. A cohomology ring is not merely a list of groups but an algebra, and the computations of the rings of projective spaces show that the ring structure distinguishes spaces whose individual homology and cohomology groups coincide. Poincare duality then closes the classical theory into a circle: the cap product isomorphism means a closed manifold's cohomology in degree k and homology in degree n minus k are two readings of one object, so a computation done cheaply in low degrees buys the high degrees for free. Chapter 4 is deliberately less satisfying, and that dissatisfaction is information. The compression lemma and cellular approximation show that maps between CW complexes can be deformed onto skeleta, which is why Whitehead's theorem can be proved at all, but the stable phenomena, Postnikov towers, and obstruction theory sketched later in the chapter mark the point where classification stops being finite. A reader who absorbs the whole arc learns to ask of any invariant three questions in order: on what class of objects is it defined, by what finite model is it computed, and at what frontier does it stop determining the object. Those three questions, asked in that order, are the book's deepest export. Applied to a reasoning engine, they become a design review checklist: every signal family should be able to state its domain, its finite computational model, and its known frontier of failure, and a family that cannot answer the third question should be treated as not yet understood, however well it performs on the cases where it has been tried. The book's own honesty about its omissions, spectral sequences deferred to a companion volume, characteristic classes to another, models the same discipline: scope is declared, not discovered by the reader at the moment of failure.
reasoning_traces.retrocausal_genealogy: The lineage runs from Riemann and Poincare, who first treated holes and winding as mathematical objects, through Brouwer's degree and fixed point work around 1910, to the algebraic formalization of the 1930s and 1940s: Hurewicz's higher homotopy groups, Eilenberg and MacLane's axiomatic homology and their semisimplicial complexes of 1950, which survive here as Delta complexes, and Whitehead's CW complexes and his theorem tying homotopy groups to homotopy type. Hatcher writes as the heir who reorganizes this inheritance geometrically, restoring the pictures that the purely algebraic mid century treatments had suppressed.
reasoning_traces.theory_of_mind: Hatcher believes the reader learns topology through geometry first and algebra second: nearly every algebraic object in the book is introduced only after a picture or a deformation has made its existence plausible, and definitions are embedded in prose rather than displayed, as if to insist they are ideas rather than formalities. His model of the domain is that intuition is a reliable guide precisely because the classical theorems were themselves discovered geometrically, and that the algebra is a bookkeeping system for deformations the reader can already see. Rigor is present everywhere but is deliberately kept in the background until the intuition needs it.
reasoning_traces.cross_layer_veto: Several results in this book veto shortcuts that other layers of a system might want to take. Homology's insensitivity to torsion in the Euler characteristic vetoes any attempt to read chi as a complete invariant. The failure of excision and van Kampen for higher homotopy groups vetoes naive divide and conquer computation of pi_n. Whitehead's theorem vetoes identifying spaces from a finite list of invariants, since all homotopy groups are required. And the non naturality of the splitting in the universal coefficient theorem vetoes treating cohomology as a functorial dual of homology: the Ext correction is compulsory, not optional.

universal_lens: Read as a general template, the book is a manual for building invariants of complicated objects: choose an equivalence relation coarser than identity but finer than uselessness, construct invariants constant on its classes, find finite models where the invariants are computable, prove the models agree with the abstract definition, and map the exact boundary where the computation rules stop working. Any field that classifies structured objects under deformation, from data analysis to program semantics, can run this same program.
gsi_mapping: For the Galaxy Sports Institute the take is methodological: this is the reference example of how a mature quantitative field organizes itself, with invariants defined before computations, hypotheses stated before theorems, and counterexamples cataloged as first class knowledge. Its treatment of local to global assembly, in van Kampen and Mayer Vietoris, is a model for how institute level research should merge partial studies, and its invariant under deformation viewpoint is the right standard for deciding when two studied systems are genuinely the same system.
gse_mapping: For the Galaxy Sports Edge engine the transferable machinery is concrete: homotopy style equivalence for canonicalizing game states, chain complex bookkeeping where boundaries are what the layer above already explains and homology is the unexplained residue, Mayer Vietoris and van Kampen overlap corrections when merging partial analyses, excision tests before dropping data from relative computations, degree style sums of signed local contributions, and Whitehead and Hurewicz style gates that say at which resolution a cheap invariant is exact and beyond which it is only a shadow.
